speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with a matter of pressing necessity.
Considering that the Bank of Canada has just lowered its prime rate to 9 per cent; that the new Quebec Minister of Finance will attend the conference of ministers of finance of Canada which will take place in a couple of months, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the Minister of Finance of Canada be accompanied by the Governor of the Bank of Canada to this conference to help Canadian Ministers of Finance to establish a long-term monetary policy for Canada with a view to promoting economic expansion and, with the co-operation of the Bank of Canada, reducing Financial pressures which increasingly tend to dismember Confederation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 43 for the following motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas the Minister of Finance informed the provinces of Canada that the five year revenue guarantee given the provinces in 1971 with reference to the new income tax legislation would be terminated at the end of 1976 and not renewed and that the formula for calculating compensation would be changed retroactively for 1974 and 1975, and whereas the Minister of Finance has now offered the provinces as compensation for the end of the revenue guarantee the transfer of one income tax point equalized to the national average, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That this House commends the government for this more equitable attitude and directs the government to cease its attempt to change the formula for compensation retroactively and meet its commitment to the provinces of Canada on the said revenue guarantee.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which, as I indicated yesterday, concerns the role of parliamentary secretaries answering, at will, questions directed to ministers or acting ministers. Yesterday, questions I asked of the acting minister of finance, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, and of the Prime Minister, were answered by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, despite the fact that repeated efforts were made to direct those questions to the acting minister of finance. These questions, in general, dealt with the intentions of the minister of bringing down a new budget, and specifically with his assessment of the economy in light of an unfavourable forecast by the OECD of the economic future of this country.
As such, these were questions of policy which in tradition, precedent and practice have been reserved for ministers and acting ministers, not parliamentary secretaries who are not privy to cabinet decisions and who do not share in the collective ministerial responsibility of government for its policies and programs.
I know that there have been exchanges on topics related to the one I am dealing with today, and I do not propose to cite examples of precedents which have already been put before Your Honour, including the precedent-as will be seen in Hansard-of October 29. I do feel, however, that budget considerations are among the clearest examples of government policy:making, and no parliamentary secretary, no matter how competent-and I stress that-can attempt to answer questions of this kind when he has no access to or responsibility for the decisions of the cabinet. If a question regarding the development of policy is asked, then the answer of a parliamentary secretary, who constitutionally has no role in discussions of policy, must of necessity be irrelevant to the question. The answer can be no more than a bland reassurance based on blissful ignorance rather than informed concern.

I noted with interest the exchange last month on this very point when the Chair indicated that in addition to the well-recognized right of hon. members of the House to ask questions, there is also no obligation to answer those questions. The Chair also stated, as reported at page 590 of Hansard:
-it is difficult to say that a mere attempt to answer on the part of the parliamentary secretary, acting minister or another acting in his stead is not an adequate response when no response is required by the rules.
Mr. Speaker, I believe you put your finger on a very important distinction which I would like to reiterate today. For example, this distinction was brought out in the book "Procedures in the Canadian House of Commons", written by Mr. Dawson. At page 158 of this book, Mr. Dawson discusses the whole question of the impact of the question period. He points out that the rules certainly contemplate that information is solicited and, hopefully, gained. But in reference to Your Honour's comment of October 29, I think Mr. Dawson's opinion is very relevant, and that opinion is expressed at page 158. Referring to the detail we solicit as far as questions are concerned, Mr. Dawson states:
This is, however, the most limited and least valuable use of the parliamentary question. There is little doubt that a letter or telephone call to a minister would produce factual information more quickly than would a question in the House. The rules, of course, ignore the real purpose of most questions. Over the years they have become the principal weapon in the hands of the opposition parties. There is little hope in their minds that they will get a major amendment accepted in the House or otherwise alter government policy significantly. They may, however, harass the government and demonstrate its deficiencies to the electorate. For this the oral parliamentary question is unequalled. The question itself must be short but each answer as it comes from the minister can be... followed to a conclusion whether that conclusion be a revelation by the government of all the significant facts, or perhaps, even more revealing, a refusal to disclose them.
I suggest that that is a fundamental reason why it has become customary that the rules provide that oral questions be put only to ministers and, as is accepted, to acting ministers. They, and they alone, should be tested in this House. I suggest that the demonstration we had in the oral question period today is a vivid demonstration. The President of the Treasury Board and the Prime Minister were under an oral question barrage which, I suggest, had a totally different effect in its outcome on this House than if that exchange had been directed to parliamentary secretaries on behalf of those two gentlemen.

In terms of information, and also of the impact on this House. I respectfully suggest that there is a significant difference between acting ministers and parliamentary secretaries. The hard fact is that the Standing Orders of this House do not allow parliamentary secretaries to answer at will, especially on matters of policy. Our Standing Orders do provide for other things, but there is no provision for having a question put to them that is asked of a minister or an acting minister who is in attendance. Acting ministers, on the other hand, do have the right to respond to questions of policy. As cabinet ministers, they take the same oath, they share in collective accountability to this House, and they can advise on the decision-making process.

The Standing Orders governing the conduct of parliamentary secretaries, and the Parliamentary Secretaries Act, are very clear on this matter: parliamentary secretaries are responsible to their ministers-the wording of the act is very clear on that-and they are not responsible to this House. Parliamentary secretaries are specifically not mentioned in reference to question period in this House, with the exception of Standing Order 40(3) to which Your Honour referred in a previous discussion concerning their role.
Standing Order 40(3) of course deals with the adjournment debate, and I would suggest, with respect, Mr. Speaker, that it is a different situation. Specifically, the Standing Order provides that a parliamentary secretary may appear and respond on behalf of his minister. I say that is different from responding during the oral question period, because obviously the minister can direct the parliamentary secretary as to what response he may see fit to make on the adjournment debate. That is entirely different, I respectfully suggest, from a parliamentary secretary gratuitously offering an answer when an acting minister declines to answer.
I would also like to say that a practice has developed precisely because the responsibilities of a parliamentary secretary are not exactly spelled out in the rules or, indeed, in precedents that are now before the House. If we allow parliamentary secretaries to respond to questions, that should not be construed as a right that they can use at will on any question being put to a minister.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that there are really three shades to all questions. If a member puts a question to a parliamentary secretary, he has obviously opted to accept the parliamentary secretary's answer, and in spite of the rules regarding such an answer, the practice has arisen in this House that the parliamentary secretary may respond to the question. Clearly, that is a practice that has arisen; but I would suggest that the rules should clarify it. If we read the rule on oral questions, Standing Order 39(5) provides as follows:
Before the orders of the day are proceeded with, questions on matters of urgency may be addressed orally to ministers of the Crown-
There is no suggestion that a parliamentary secretary has the right to receive a question, or that we have the right to put a question to a parliamentary secretary, but I am saying that the practice has arisen. I would say that if members on this side of the House wish to direct a question to a parliamentary secretary, that is their option. The distinction I wish to make is the alternative situation where a member on this side of the House directs a question to a minister or acting minister. I would suggest there is absolutely no precedent for this; it is something that has become a practice. There is nothing in the rules that allows a parliamentary secretary to stand in his place and respond.
I suggest that an acting minister or minister has two choices when queried in the House: he can answer as he sees fit, or he cannot answer, and let hon. members judge as they will. But I suggest that ministers cannot duck questions by allowing parliamentary secretaries to speak for them when the questions

are not directed to a parliamentary secretary. I suggest that if a member of the House puts a question to a parliamentary secretary, that is an entirely different thing because the hon. member has opted to take that course.
I have searched for precedents in our parliamentary manuals dealing with this situation, but unfortunately I cannot find a clearcut precedent for what we are directing ourselves to today. I was able to find some references in the British House of Commons when they had something like a parliamentary secretary system-they do not have it currently, because they use junior ministers-and I did find that there are clear precedents where what happened yesterday was taken exception to in the House of Commons when they had something like the parliamentary secretary system.

I would suggest this is perhaps an example of where this type of situation has arisen in the British House, and clearly it was felt that if it is a question of policy, and a person who is not in the government attempts to respond, he should be stopped because he has no such right. Certainly, it should be open to the member putting the question to say if he wishes to accept the answer of a parliamentary secretary because an acting minister or minister declines to answer.
In view of what I have stated, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is fundamentally important to this House that the cabinet remain responsible, certainly during oral question period, to members of the House. As Your Honour has pointed out, this is a rather unique function in our parliamentary procedure in Canada. I believe it is imperative, bearing in mind that we have 32 members of cabinet, that we insist that only cabinet ministers respond when hon. members on this side direct their questions to a minister or acting minister, and that a parliamentary secretary should be held to have no right to stand and answer as a substitute for a minister. If you find that I have a prima facie case of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That the matter of parliamentary secretaries answering questions not addressed to them and concerning which they can constitutionally have no knowledge, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

-than were given by the parliamentary secretary yesterday. Indeed, they are a model of information and we, having heard so much about the necessity for this government to give information, find it rather bizarre to hear an argument today that such extensive information should not be provided to the House.
I would refer to three points made by the hon. member, and I think I do not misstate his case if I put them this way. First, he says that a parliamentary secretary is not adequately informed. Second, he says that a parliamentary secretary is not responsible in some constitutional sense; and, third, he says that the Standing Orders do not provide for parliamentary secretaries to respond to oral questions. One assumes that the gravamen of his complaint is that the use of parliamentary secretaries is in some ways an attempt by the government to thwart the opposition's attempt to obtain information. To deal with the fourth ground, the answer as recorded in Hansard, at pages 1324 and 1325 is the best answer, and nothing more need be said.
May I deal with the first point. A parliamentary secretary, while not sharing in the collective responsibility for the making of policy that belongs to the cabinet alone, has access to virtually the same information on the administration of the department as does the minister. Parliamentary secretaries, including my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for York Centre, frequently attend departmental meetings, and when they are substituting for their ministers during the question period are briefed by the same officers and given the same material. While it is true that parliamentary secretaries cannot attend the full cabinet, they may well from time to time participate in cabinet committees and may also properly be given access to some cabinet papers. If the complaint is that by not being part of the group collectively responsible for policy, parliamentary secretaries cannot answer questions on policy, the response is to be found in the rules of the House as set out in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, citation 171, which reads in part:
A question oral or written must not...
(w) raise a matter of policy too large to be dealt with in the limits of an
answer to a question ...
(bb) ask the government's opinion on matters of policy ...
(gg) seek information about matters which are in their nature secret, such as
decisions or proceedings of cabinet.
The answer lies in the proceedings of this House. On questions of that kind the parliamentary secretary is disenti-

tied to comment on cabinet proceedings. Indeed, it is improper to ask him questions which would require him to do so, and it is improper to ask anyone questions of that kind. Notwithstanding the argument of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, the purpose of an oral question is to seek information about the administration of government, and there is no reason why a parliamentary secretary cannot provide such information as readily as the minister. In support of that position, may I again refer to the responses made yesterday.
Perhaps the hon. member for York-Simcoe and his colleagues would like to change the rules in order to have mini-debates at this hour of the day. Perhaps they are not interested in the provision regarding the giving of information to the House. However, the rules we have been following are presently in existence. We have followed the widespread practice in this House of having parliamentary secretaries respond to questions, and I say that from experience in this House extending back nearly 14 years. Indeed, in the current session of parliament we have seen questions directed by opposition members to parliamentary secretaries in the observed absence of a minister. Clearly, the practice of having parliamentary secretaries respond to questions is well established and has been for a long time under our procedures.
Second, I deal with the point as to whether a parliamentary secretary is responsible in the constitutional sense. While a parliamentary secretary is not constitutionally responsible to parliament in the same sense as a minister, he is responsible to his minister, who is, in turn, responsible to parliament for the behaviour of his parliamentary secretary in his capacity as parliamentary secretary. Parliamentary secretaries are obliged to take oaths of office, including an oath of administrative secrecy, just as are other departmental officials and ministers who are responsible to parliament for their official behaviour. The right hon. member for Prince Albert is my authority for this theory. He espoused it as long ago as February 9, 1954, when he said, as reported at page 1909 of the House of Commons Debates for that year:
-I can scarcely believe that it would ever have been contemplated that they speak without responsibility.
When the right hon. member was prime minister he was reminded of that statement, and on March 16, 1960, said, as reported at page 2129 of the House of Commons Debates for that year:
Mr. Speaker, that is still my view.
Parliamentary secretaries, of course, have a greater degree of freedom than their ministers in the sense that their restraints, in terms of departmental responsibility, are confined to that department and they have the freedom of debate and action which is outside that imposed by the collegial system of cabinet.
Third, may I deal with the point that the rules only provide for questions to be answered by ministers. I have pointed out that the observed practice of this House has for a long period of time been the opposite. The hon. member clearly founded his argument on the assumption that unless a right is specifically and positively given by the Standing Orders of the

House, it does not exist. I think that to state it in that way is to refute the proposition. Hon. members know that many things in the parliamentary firmament are not to be found within the covers of our provisional Standing Orders; they know, indeed, that there is a widespread practice and procedure reaching far back into the practices of the British parliament in this regard-and, of course, we have built up a substantial practice of our own. I therefore say that if the hon. member's argument is to succeed, and if hon. members are to be confined to the specific words of the Standing Orders, he will have won a Pyrrhic victory indeed, because the fundamental rights of all members of parliament will have been withdrawn by that particular argument.
Section 3 of the Parliamentary Secretaries Act reads in part:
The parliamentary secretary or secretaries to a minister shall assist the minister in such manner as the minister directs.
This gives ministers authority to direct parliamentary secretaries to do anything not otherwise prohibited. Since there is no Standing Order prohibiting parliamentary secretaries from answering questions, clearly, in accordance with statute law, they may be directed to do so. This view is so clearly established that it was referred to by yourself, Mr. Speaker, twice, in your opinion of November 5, 1974, and again on November 15, 1974. Perhaps I need not refer in extenso to that admirable opinion. May I, however, quote a few lines of it. Your Honour, as reported, said:
Similarly, the privilege, of course, of being elevated to the position of parliamentary secretary falls only on those hon. members, not only the recognition, prestige and advantage that comes from their position but the obligation of answering questions, because not only do they occasionally answer questions during the question period, but they do so on a regular basis during the "late show" proceedings at 10 p.m. when they answer for the ministry. I have taken the position, to which I hold, that those who are clothed with the responsibility of answering for the government ought not to use the time of the question period for the privilege of asking questions of the government.
That was the reverse proposition in relation to parliamentary secretaries. Further, on November 15, 1974, Your Honour said, as reported:
-the parliamentary secretary is proposing to give information on behalf of her minister which, as I think I have said on previous occasions, is a very important aspect of the work of parliamentary secretaries.
That, Mr. Speaker, I think could be regarded as the summum optimum of wisdom on this particular question. Indeed, it would be detaining the House unnecessarily to try to improve on such, if I may use another official language, sagesse. I merely say, in conclusion, that it has been widely established in the House that with the current expansion of the administrative responsibilities of government, parliamentary secretaries may answer questions both written and oral. I would sustain the sound statement made by the Chair in the past, a position which I maintain would be upheld as reflecting on the better management of the House and the government of Canada.

The one point I should like to emphasize is the matter of courtesy. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe suggested, if a member, in the absence of the minister, asks the parliamentary secretary a question, there can be no complaint. However, when a private member goes to the trouble of finding out who the acting minister is-it is not a great deal of trouble; I have the list in my pocket every day-and asks the acting minister to answer a question, and without anything being said by that acting minister it is passed over to the parliamentary secretary, it is something less than full courtesy.
I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe will have trouble sustaining his point procedurally in getting a ruling from Your Honour in his way, but I do want to make this point. There would be less difficulty in the question period if we had a little more courtesy as to who answers the questions. This is not only true about parliamentary secretaries answering when we put questions to acting ministers; it is also true on the part of the Prime Minister. On many a day when we think a question is important enough for him to answer it, he waves to someone else. That is my point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ORGANIZATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY-DATE LETTER OF RESIGNATION OF MR. CARON RECEIVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the NDP House leader's allusion to the minister's use of the rules in terms of courtesy. It reminded me of the story of the lawyer who was advising a young student: he said when the law was in his favour, he should pound the judge; when the facts were in his favour, he should pound the jury. But when neither the law nor the facts were in his favour, he should pound the table, and perhaps the witness, from time to time. I endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre with regard to courtesy in terms of the operation of the House of Commons. By doing that, I do not also endorse what he said with regard to the position that Your Honour ought to take.
Your Honour knows that I feel very strongly about the matter. I argued it in the House very strenuously a few weeks
Oral Questions
ago. I do not intend to repeat that argument today. Your Honour did not come to a decision with respect to the matter at that time. I want to speak to a couple of points made by the Minister of Finance. One of his weakest arguments was that the increase in volume of administrative matters made it necessary for parliamentary secretaries to deal with certain matters. That is no argument at all. It may well be an argument for the fact that the rules of the House have not kept up with administrative practice, but it is certainly not an argument for the point of view he wished to advance.
With regard to the adjournment debate, I have tried to make it clear that the Standing Orders are quite different in terms of the responsibility of a parliamentary secretary. In fact, they specifically pinpoint the parliamentary secretary as one to whom responsibility can be delegated in terms of the adjournment debate. I do not have the rules in front of me, and I did go through them the last time. There is, however, a significant omission with regard to the functions in the balance of the rules.
The next argument advanced by the minister was with regard to the statute establishing parliamentary secretaries. He was quite right with respect to what it says, but we have to look beyond what it says to see what it means. Surely, the statute ought not to be interpreted to stand outside something that falls within the jurisdiction of the rules of the House of Commons. Surely, the act was not meant to be interpreted to say that notwithstanding parliamentary practice, procedure and traditions, many of which are not written, a minister of the Crown, by mere delegation of some function to his parliamentary secretary, can transgress the rules of the House.
I respectfully suggest that the practice of the House has been rather loose; it ought to be tightened up. The rules which ought to govern in terms of practice clearly indicate that ministers answer questions in the House of Commons, or acting ministers, not parliamentary secretaries except in that very limited way in accordance with our rules. I do not intend this to be a criticism of the Chair, but it is a practice which has developed over a long period of time.
What I conceive to be the rules have been breached by not being regarded because of convenience. In my judgment, one of those conveniences is somewhat contrary to the rules; that is the practice of opposition members putting questions to parliamentary secretaries. In my respectful submission, that ought not to be done. If it is being done now as a matter of practice, that practice ought not to be honoured by omitting to change the rules or interpreting the rules in such a way that the interpretation goes against the written word of the law in this House of Commons. In other words, I am saying that if the practice is to continue, the rules ought to be changed. The interpretation that the Chair may give to the rules ought not to be contrary to the written rules.
I wish to deal with the last argument, the question of ministerial responsibility. There is a direct responsibility of ministers, certainly among themselves and to the House of Commons. However, the fallacy of advancing one more step and moving that responsibility to the parliamentary secretary

November 25, 1976

was demonstrated by the minister himself when he said that the parliamentary secretary is responsible to the minister, in turn, who is responsible to the House of Commons. On its face, that indicates that the responsibility is one step removed, that there is no direct responsibility between the parliamentary secretary and the House of Commons. That responsibility is intended by the rules to be that of a minister except in the case of the adjournment debate.
The questions of the other day which gave rise to this question of privilege were very important. I do not suggest, nor would I suggest, that in answering those questions the parliamentary secretary followed the parliamentary practice improperly. He answered them very well. He gave the House the fullest possible information.
If we are to maintain the relationship that ought to exist in this House in terms of answering questions on policy matters, then I suggest, unlike the hon. member for York-Simcoe, that the rules ought to be strictly observed and that either ministers or acting ministers, who were surely named for a purpose, answer those questions. If the hon. member for York-Simcoe is prepared to say that if he chooses to ask a parliamentary secretary a question, he should be allowed to do so, that is his position. I happen to disagree with it. I have a little tougher position in terms of ministerial responsibility. However, we perhaps ought to look at that.
If Your Honour accepts the argument in terms of what the Standing Orders of this House say, it is my respectful submission that there is a question of privilege. The privilege is the right of members of parliament to represent their constituencies and constituents in terms of obtaining what can be judged by practice, precedent, oath and responsibility as matters that are of record on the part of a minister. A ministerial answer in this House of Commons with respect to a matter of government policy is different in its nature and essence than an answer by any other member of this House. However well endowed with knowledge that member may be, it is different in parliamentary terms, and it is different in terms of accountability. Frankly, I think the rule ought to be strictly, rather than loosely, construed-and if there is doubt at all, that doubt ought to be resolved in favour of preserving the traditions of the House, not in permitting other usage. In this respect I must say that I disagree with some of my colleagues. This is not to say we ought not to consider changes, but the rules are before us and are to be followed. As we go down the road in this and succeeding parliaments, this question will have an important bearing on the manner in which ministers and hon. members generally conduct themselves during the question period.
I did not intend to be so long, Mr. Speaker, but the subject is an important one, and in that spirit I am pleased to support the idea which the hon. member for York-Simcoe has advanced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

The Minister of Finance has advanced solid arguments for your consideration, Mr. Speaker. I did not

intend to intervene at all until the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put forward an argument which he characterized as a "rather softer argument" dealing with the question of courtesy. I wish to put forward another "soft argument" which I believe ought to be given at least as much weight as the argument advanced by the hon. member.
Very often, a question addressed to the ministry contains damaging and dangerous innuendos. Questions are often heavily laden with false premises. These statements are made; they are before the House; they are a matter of record. If the minister is absent, the acting minister may often not have had the opportunity to be as fully informed as the minister himself would have been; he may not even be in a position to contradict false assumptions or set the record straight in connection with some of the allegations contained in a question asked. In these circumstances it is very valuable for a parliamentary secretary to be able to stand up and at least correct the record, even if he is not in a position at the time to outline a policy. Very often, though, he is in a position to give the same answer as the minister would have given had he been present.
Yesterday, for example, there was an allegation that the OECD had characterized Canada's current economic performance as a "mini-recession". There are no grounds for that allegation, and I was glad to be able to stand in my place and set the record straight on the question. Had I been unable to do so, the acting minister responsible for the portfolio in the House that day might not have been in a position to make such a correction, simply because he might not have had the opportunity a parliamentary secretary often has to be briefed by officials and be prepared to deal with the kind of allegation and innuendo which should not accompany questions but which, unfortunately, so often does.
Before resuming my seat, I want to make one observation on the submission made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. He suggested that Your Honour was being invited to ignore written rules contained in the Standing Orders by extending some privilege or other to parliamentary secretaries. I do not know what written rule or order the hon. member was referring to. None was cited. As far as I can see, there is no written rule or order which denies parliamentary secretaries the right to answer questions during the question period.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ORGANIZATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY-DATE LETTER OF RESIGNATION OF MR. CARON RECEIVED
speechtext:
To deal with a few of the points which have been raised, let me say, first, that there can be no doubt about the truth of the proposition we have just heard. If the practice of parliamentary secretaries rising to answer questions during the question period is to be stopped, for whatever reason, they would have to be freed from the bonds I have placed upon them in this parliament not to put questions to ministers. That is the easiest part of the problem before me.
This matter has been put forward by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. It concerns the application of the rules and precedents as they apply to the procedures we must follow during the question period. As such, it is clearly a matter of order, and not a question of privilege. However, I think it would be disrespectful to the hon. member for York-Simcoe and others who have taken part in this discussion to brush the matter aside simply because it is not really a question of privilege. It is a point of order which has been raised twice recently. On each occasion, extensive and weighty arguments were put forward on both sides. There are, of course, difficulties which have to be faced. The hon. member for York-Simcoe suggested there might be circumstances in which parliamentary secretaries could answer questions, and other circumstances in which they ought not to be allowed to do so.
With all respect to the hon. member, that situation would be an impossible one for the Chair to resolve on a moment to moment basis. There are enough of those situations as things are now. The hon. member certainly raised one fundamental point, that is, whether in answer to questions-and this aspect was touched on rather ably, too, by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton-a minister who is absent is bound by an answer given by his parliamentary secretary.
It has been my suggestion in the past that an effort be made to resolve this question before the procedure committee. However, I am not in the position to order that this be done. Indeed, I take as well-founded the approach of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton that a strict interpretation of the Standing Orders might lead us to the conclusion that, at least pro tern and until there is some other resolution, parliamentary secretaries do not have the right to answer questions. That, to my mind, may be one interpretation of the Standing Orders, but it is a strict one and is certainly not in keeping with our recent practice. For the moment, I would like to reserve judgment on the matter. I do take this to be a serious point of order and it is one on which I shall make a decision as soon as possible. I shall actively explore the possibility of

having the procedure committee look at this question on an agreed basis. If that is not possible by agreement, I shall have to make a decision from the chair, and I shall do this as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The House will recall that very near the conclusion of the discussion yesterday, a motion was put forward in respect of which the Chair reserved its ruling on procedural acceptability in order that argument might be presented on resumption of the debate today. The sponsor of the motion was the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan). Because this is a reasoned amendment to the second reading motion, it raises a number of very well known procedural difficulties. I would be pleased to hear some discussion, since the Chair certainly has very serious reservations about the acceptability of this motion as a reasoned amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your comments, and I appreciate the fact that the vitality of reasoned amendments in this House has been rather shaky, to say the least, since many have been moved and few have been called or recognized. However, I rely on my basic philosophy that hope does spring eternal. I have also tried to recognize or perceive, in the amendment I have proposed, the fundamental ingredients. As I understand it, there are basically two ingredients which would allow a reasoned amendment. I realize there are relatively few positions and that this is a relatively narrow situation, but I suggest there are two elements in issue regarding the reasoned amendment which I raised yesterday.

November 25, 1976

The first question is whether the proposed amendment relates to a recognized principle and opposes it. The second question is whether the amendment is relevant to the bill. I suggest that it does involve a principle, and that it is relevant. As I said yesterday, and repeat now, there is a very important principle at stake here. Bill C-19 in many ways is an attempt to cut expenditures by lopping off parts of long-established programs to the extent that, following passage of this bill- assuming it does pass-these programs and their related funds will be determined by ministers and bureaucrats, and not by the House of Commons.
I cannot really trespass too far in my argument in respect of this motion in the area of the Auditor General's report, as that is outside the bill and cannot be used to fortify my argument. However, as Your Honour well knows, the only reason this institution was created was to exercise some control over the public purse, rather than to become the legislative chamber it has become. It is for this reason that the Auditor General's report and the implementation of this bill are so fundamental.
I attempted to draft my reasoned amendment in a way that would highlight and include what I think are the important elements. This bill, in its several clauses, terminates certain programs and alters others in areas of family allowances and industrial research incentives. I do not have the bill in front of me, but clause 15 repeals section 272 of the Railway Act. It includes a number of things outside the protection of the statute and thus outside the area of scrutiny and comment by the press and members of this place. It takes a number of things away from the protection of the statute and puts them into the area of orders in council or ministerial discretion.
This is the principle I tried to cover by my reasoned amendment, that is, the bill changes things from statute to order in council; it does away with the protection of the statute and puts things at the mercy of ministerial or discretion. I do not suggest that is necessarily a negative thing, because ministerial discretion is a necessary and normal exercise. However, in view of the fact that many of these programs and their future will be continued on the basis of whim, this question definitely involves something that is substantive. If this chamber is to continue to function as it has in the past, we must do something to provide protection in terms of these legislative programs.
What I intend to say from now on will be in a somewhat negative vein. An omnibus bill such as C-19 takes many things out of the statutes. This is accomplished either by repealing the statutes or by continuing their function by order in council, by ministerial discretion or by bureaucratic control. In that way we lessen the importance of the function of this institution-and that is the principle that is involved. Bill C-19 is a relatively short bill. I initially considered the bill carefully in an attempt to find the principle, so I could outline to Your Honour in a very few minutes certain things that should seriously be considered.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
The next question is, assuming there is a principle, is it relevant? I say here that the whole essence of this institution, in its creation, was to control the public purse, to take the old king and shake him down a little and say to him that he cannot fight the war of the crusades today and that we will not give him a few horses because we do not like the cause he supports. That is how we all met. Your Honour knows that is how you were dragged up to the chair when you were first appointed.
Actually, I have the ingredients of a great speech here, Mr. Speaker, because you know how you were dragged from the corner and we elected you, and you were appointed unanimously to be our number one commoner sitting in the chair. You know that your predecessors had their heads chopped off up until the year 1200. Sometimes, when we sit here in frustration during the question period, we think about other beheadings we would like to have from time to time. But we do not do it that way any more. The essence of the matter is that the Speaker and the institution of commoners met behind closed doors and would not let the king come in, because every time he came in he trampled on the commoners and usually tried to get the Speaker and chop off his head and float the head down the river Thames. That is the history of this place. By a slow, insidious process because of the complexity of society and/or the complications of government and society, it is a heck of a lot easier to be managerial and to create bills which give more and more ministerial discretion. That is just another inroad, in terms of parliamentary control, that this institution loses by Bill C-19.
In essence, and in conclusion, I say that there is the principle of parliamentary control versus ministerial discretion and those two, I suggest, are in opposition. The second thing I suggest in respect of my reasoned amendment is that is it relevant. I certainly suggest, Mr. Speaker, as would any member of this House, that with the good bureaucrats and public servants we have, with the torchlight and spotlight of the press, and with the scrutiny of commoners in examining ministers across the floor, we can exercise restraint on government expenditures a heck of a lot better if this question is debated on the floor of the House than if it is all done by the stroke of a pen in exercising ministerial discretion.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I have introduced my reasoned amendment. I shall not say anything more at this late hour of the day, except that I believe the amendment, as drafted, with these principles which are so fundamental and necessary, is an amendment which could be just a little exception to the previous precedents in this House, and thus find favour with Your Honour.

The measure was presented during the first session of the thirtieth parliament and on that occasion was discussed at considerable length. The House has had a considerable time in which to analyse this legislation and debate it on the floor of the House of Commons.
I think that as a matter of background it is relevant to point out that while this bill is complicated, and in fact is an omnibus measure which affects a number of different programs and statutes, nevertheless, a number of members of the House during the course of the debate have expressed concern that perhaps some of the speeches were straying rather dramatically from the point and perhaps the subject matter of those speeches was, at best, only tenuously connected to the subject matter of the legislation.
I simply say that the matter has received extensive consideration, perhaps consideration going beyond the precise nature of the bill, which is a restraint of expenditures bill relating to a certain number of very specific programs of the government. It seems to me, that the amendment now being proposed as a "reasoned amendment" by my hon. friend from Annapolis

Valley perhaps falls into the same mould as a great deal of the discussion into which, unfortunately, this House has already fallen; that is, it strays rather far from the point of this piece of legislation which is intended, in its result, to save in the order of $250 million in government expenditures only, of course, if this bill can be passed with dispatch.
As a matter of reference, I should like to refer to May's nineteenth edition, pages 499 and 500, where this point is discussed at considerable length. I shall not take the time of the House to read the citation from May's but will simply point out that there the learned author notes three specific points which would cause a motion of the nature which has been proposed to be defective. One of those reasons is relevancy. The motion must be relevant to the subject matter of the bill and, indeed, if it is irrelevant, or not strictly relevant, it is out of order, according to May in his writing on this point.
Second, the learned author points out that the amendment must not be concerned in detail with the provisions of the bill. In other words, at the second reading stage it has to relate to the subject matter in principle and must not anticipate an amendment which could be dealt with at a later stage during committee consideration of the bill. Third, May points out that the amendment cannot amount to simply a direct negation of the principle of the bill itself.
I submit to you, sir, that the amendment which has been proposed is defective on at least two of the three counts described in the nineteenth edition of May at pages 499 and 500.
The first problem, I suggest, is the question of relevancy. It seems to me, as I pointed out in my general preamble, that Bill C-19 deals specifically with the reduction of government expenditures. That is the dominant theme of the legislation as indicated in the short title and as repeated constantly throughout the statute. It is not a bill dealing with ministerial discretion-and that, I submit, is the gist of the proposed amendment-but, rather, a bill dealing with the question of the restraint of expenditures for government programs.
I heard the point made by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley, that in some fashion the point of ministerial discretion relates to the matter of restraint of expenditures, or at least to the over-all authority of parliament to scrutinize government expenditures, and he outlined some elaborate historical background for that proposition. But I submit that he cannot make the argument that an assumption of ministerial discretion necessarily implies a diminution of the authority of parliament to scrutinize and control the expenditures of government.
I certainly do not believe that the reasoned amendment, relating, as it does, so directly and almost exclusively to the question of ministerial discretion, can be relevant to the bill which, in effect, deals with restraint of government expenditures. I submit that these are two separate things which perhaps can be knitted together in a historical pattern, if one wants to put together the history of the particular matter, but I am not sure that one can then make the argument that this is
November 25, 1976

a relevant amendment; and I submit to Your Honour that it is, in fact, irrelevant on that ground.
I also have concern about the second point which is made by May, that is, that the amendment must not be concerned in detail with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which might be moved in committee. It seems to me that if my hon. friend is concerned about some of the phrases in Bill C-19 which apparently call upon a minister to exercise a judgment or to make some assessment of a situation and act upon it, then he is doing precisely what May says he cannot do in a reasoned amendment. He is anticipating a detail of the bill and particularly a matter which might be dealt with by amendment in committee. On those two grounds, both in relation to the matter of relevancy and in relation to the question of anticipating an amendment, or dealing with a detail of the bill, I submit to Your Honour that the proposed amendment does not properly fall within the category of a reasoned amendment, and therefore is out of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the parliamentary secretary intended to mislead the House but, as I recollect, what he said at the beginning was that the bill was before parliament and had been debated in the House previously. According to my recollection, it was Bill C-87 in the first session of the thirtieth parliament which was on the order paper but was not debated on second reading. There had been extensive discussions between representatives of the official opposition and the government with respect, I think, to a clause of the bill, in the hope that the government would drop it, which might have had some effect on that piece of legislation; but the matter was not debated at the time, and Bill C-19 is the first time the subject matter has been debated in the House.

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned last evening I had just commenced my comments with respect to Bill C-19 and, as I indicated at the outset, although in my opinion there was ample opportunity for individuals in this debate to look at those areas where there has been excessive government spending, it was relevant, also, to comment on the Auditor General's report with respect to the whole area of government spending and management of money.
I also indicated that I believe there are several aspects of the bill which deserve to be explored to a greater degree and in greater detail. For example, I pointed out the difficulties with respect to Information Canada, and the fact that that program had been a failure despite the fact that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), during the debate on November 8, attempted to mislead the House, in my view, by implying that the program had been discontinued as a measure of restraint and because of criticism from the opposition. This I am not prepared to accept. I gave an illustration of the failure of Information Canada, and referred specifically to the role which that body was presumably to have played and which it failed to do.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
The next point which I mentioned yesterday before the House adjourned concerned that section of the bill which deals with amendments to the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act. I pointed out that this act was introduced in March, 1967, and although one could have found substantial evidence from the programs emanating from that act to justify its continuation, I believe the issue was far more basic and required more than simply amending the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act; that the basic issue was the government's lack of response to the call for a science policy for Canada.
Numerous questions had been put in the House of Commons, and in fact opposition days had been devoted specifically to the subject matter of medical research and the ministry of science and technology. I pointed out that after the throne speech of 1973, a number of us in the House had great hopes that perhaps the government of the day had finally seen fit to establish a science policy for Canada, not only in human but in economic terms. From subsequent actions of the government or, if I may say, lack of action by the government, we have seen that this proposed program has not been implemented.
Just before the adjournment yesterday I referred to a recent representation by a very learned body in Canada, the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies, pointing out that this group of individuals will be coming to Ottawa on December 7 and 8 to meet members of parliament from all sides of the House. I said that this was not a special interest body, but a cross-section of numerous scientific disciplines, including such bodies as the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies, the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation, the Humanities Research Council, the Social Sciences Research Council, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Association of Physicists, the Chemical Institute of Canada, and other learned bodies-all making a really concerted effort to point out the importance and the need for a science policy for Canada and a need for some direction from the government in this area.
Mr. Speaker, in that letter they attempted very succinctly and concisely to define the theme they will be presenting to this government and members of parliament from all parties. I want to repeat that theme, which was really broken down into three parts. Reading from the letter dated November 18, 1976, the first part is this:
We seek, for all research areas, at least a restoration of the purchasing power of federal research support to the peak levels of the early 70's, at which time we took on many long term financial and other commitments which are increasingly difficult to meet.
The second point they made is as follows:
It is crucial that federally-supported research programmes have a more stable environment. To this end ... we seek some formula which would guarantee research funding over a long period rather than leaving it to the annual vagaries of parliament... We need a national policy on science. We desperately need revisions of the legislation surrounding at least two of the three federal granting councils (NRC and Canada Council) and a clear policy statement on the level of research capability which the government intends to maintain in Canada.

Restraint of Government Expenditures
The third point they made regarding the theme which will be brought to Ottawa is as follows:
On the question of priorities, we stress our willingness to engage in any analysis of areas which would be most suited to special development. We have some concerns about the best climate in which to do this, and will discuss these concerns during the lobby.
I cannot overemphasize the importance of the attitude of the government toward research in recent years. As I indicated, in 1973 many of us had high expectations as to what would happen in the whole area of science with respect to the re-establishment or redefinition of the science and technology portfolio, and yet, as has been pointed out many times in this House in debates on opposition days, really this portfolio has suddenly fallen into oblivion.
There is another clause in the bill which has not received the attention it should and, above all, there has not been an adequate explanation on the part of the government. I refer to that portion of the bill which deals with adult occupational training or specifically, the Adult Occupational Training Act. I can assure hon. members, from personal experience, that I am well aware of many positive aspects which have resulted from the program, but without some further clarification from the government I am concerned that the amendments we see in the legislation before us may be self-defeating.
When the former president of the treasury board was discussing this clause of the bill, he indicated that the cancellation of indexing of the training allowance and changes in the selection criteria would lead to a saving of $20 million in the Canada Manpower budget. As I understand the proposed changes in Bill C-19, they will permit the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) to adjust the rates paid to adults under the Adult Occupational Training Act. It is my understanding that these changes were promoted to overcome the high vacancy rate which was created either by those not taking the program or, equally important, by a significantly large number who were dropping out of the program after they had been involved with it.
These positions appear to be contradictory. On the one hand we have the former president of the treasury board indicating that there will be substantial savings of taxpayers' dollars, and on the other hand we see amendments permitting the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to review the rates at which training allowances are payable, ostensibly to correct the vacancy rate to which I have alluded. This, to me, implies that there will be an increase in the expenditure of money.
It is extremely important, during this debate, for the minister clearly to define the intent of the new regulations. If it is, in fact, the intention of the government to reorganize the administration of the program which would lead to cuts in the budget, such an approach is obviously acceptable and desirable. If, however, the government intends to decrease its services and reduce the number of people receiving Canada Manpower training, I suggest, in all honesty, that this may lead to unnecessary hardships for those who can least afford them. If it is the intention of the government to shift the program so that the only alternative is unemployment insur-

ance or welfare, as this suggests, it will obviously be counterproductive and costly and in no way will it be a restraint measure as suggested by the legislation and by the government. It is apparent to me that this aspect of the bill needs much closer examination, and a far more detailed explanation on the part of the government is necessary to justify its presence in the legislation, not only in terms of restraint but, as I indicated before, also in terms of the human and social components attached to it.
The clause of this bill which I find most objectionable and which really reflects the fuzziness of the thinking of the government is that dealing with the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act, or what is commonly referred to as the maritimes and east subsidy. As previous speakers have indicated, this clause would have very serious implications on numerous regions in Canada, and from personal contact with people in my area I have found that there will be severe hardship experienced.
As others have indicated, the subsidy applies to the movement of export flour and/or grain from inland terminals situated along Georgian Bay, Lake Huron, Prescott, Colling-wood, Midland, Goderich, Owen Sound, Sarnia, Port Col-borne, Toronto and Kingston to the ports of Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick. In addition, there are also ports in the province of Quebec which would be affected by this clause. As 1 indicated a moment or so ago, I have been in contact with those in my area who will be adversely affected by the sudden discontinuation of this subsidy. There are those who will say that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in his recent announcements made some concessions with respect to this clause, but my interpretation of what the minister has said is that nothing has effectively changed. The repeal of this section still leaves the industry in an adverse and uneconomic position: the effects will be devastating in my area. For example, I know of one mill in my area which exports approximately one-third of its business. It is obvious that the repeal of this section, without consultation and without an alternative program, could cause the company to which I am referring to lose at least one-third of its market. Obviously, this will severely cripple that industry and may well cause it to go into bankruptcy or destroy it. This will add to the existing unemployment problems in the area. Other hon. members have discussed the implications of repealing section 272 of the Railway Act, Mr. Speaker. I want to join them as strenuously as I can in opposing this clause of the bill which has implications far more serious than has been indicated by the minister in this debate.
I think it is important to look back to 1961 and some of the basic reasons for implementing the legislation on the at and east subsidy. I say that the reasons are as valid for the retention of that section today as they were for introducing the at and east subsidy in 1961. If one looks at it very carefully, the reason for promoting that legislation in 1961 is in many respects far more critical than it is at the present time. There was recognition at that time that the maritimes were confront-
November 25, 1976

ed with regional disparity and that an important tool available to the government to correct that type of regional disparity was transportation. In 1961, there was an obvious need to encourage the use of eastern ports and to assist Canadian flour companies to retain a portion of competitiveness in world markets.
Surely those conditions exist today. There is a need to promote and assist development of the expansion of the Canadian grain industry and to benefit our economy by providing mills, transportation and port employment, as well as helping the Canadian balance of trade position in manufactured goods. All these reasons which were utilized in 1961 for the introduction and implementation of that legislation are as valid today as they were then.
I have not seen convincing evidence that the government is able to refute the relevancy of those principles today. More important, they have not introduced an alternative program that will ensure the economic viability of the components to which I have alluded. The government has attempted to oversimplify the problem with their oft-repeated reference to the user-pay concept. No one denies the theoretical appeal of such a concept. I want to suggest, however, in all sincerity, that it does not reflect the regional differences in Canada and the necessity to provide assistance where services are important to meet specific national goals.
I have no intention of adding to the many examples given by other members, including the Crowsnest pass rates; but we must remember that transportation is a very valuable tool that can be, and has been used by government to correct regional disparity in this country.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) has indicated that the continuation of the at and east rail subsidy is unlikely to reverse or stem the decline in flour exports which has been apparent for several years. I would suggest that he has failed to say that by removing the subsidy, a difficult problem will become impossible. In my opinion, the federal government is prepared to abandon a very critical and important segment of our economy. In my opinion, the Canadian National Millers' Association put the problem in perspective in February of this year in a document which defines the difficulties experienced by the industry and the necessity of maintaining this subsidy until an alternative plan is available-and I think it is important to emphasize the phrase "an alternative plan is available".
Briefly, they pointed out that the U.S.S.R. had indicated a need for 375,000 tons of Canadian flour during 1976 and had called for further negotiations to be conducted in the event that freight rates are increased. The U.S.S.R. has indicated that Canada is no longer competitive in world markets and that future price increases will require them to look very carefully for alternate suppliers. I think the implications of this are apparent in terms of Canadian industry. They also pointed out that from 1954 to 1974, world demand for flour had increased by 50 per cent-and during that period Canada's share of the trade had declined from 31 per cent to 11 per cent in 1974.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
I find it difficult to believe that the government has failed to recognize that the world flour market is fiercely competitive due to the implementation of subsidy programs by many foreign governments. This government is not only failing to adopt alternative programs but, given our competitive position, in my opinion, they are now prepared to strangle the industry with the removal of the subsidy. In addition, they pointed out that some markets for grain can only be met by the export of flour where there is no milling capacity in the importing countries. The loss of subsidy will impair competitiveness and risk the loss of these most important markets.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There was a discussion on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) and on the subject of reasoned amendments at second reading stage generally. The references to May's nineteenth edition are very valuable, and I had an opportunity overnight to examine them, and again just now.
I think all hon. members understand that there is a very high mortality rate, as described by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley, with these kinds of amendments, for the simple reason that a number of actions can be taken by a member at second reading stage of a bill, the most effective one being to oppose the bill in debate, oppose it in the vote by opposing the second reading motion or voting against it, or opposing it in discussion. That, of course, negates progress of the bill and, in turn, negates the principle associated with the bill and gives all hon. members an opportunity to express their reasons for so doing.
There are, of course, a number of other motions related to the progress of the bill itself. Those are well known and need not be discussed here. The reason it is difficult to frame a reasoned amendment is that since all hon. members have the opportunity to speak against the bill and the principle of the bill, and with their vote to oppose the progress of the bill, it ought not to be given to members simply to use a reasoned amendment to put on the record their reasons for speaking against the second reading motion or their reasons for voting against the second reading motion. Those reasons fall into a very special category, and those categories are very thoroughly discussed in the well known precedents cited during the course of argument; that is to say, a simply expanded negative ought not to be accepted as a reasoned amendment.
There are rules of relevancy, as with all amendments at all stages. On two counts I have some difficulty with the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley. In the first place, the declaration which he cites is, in my opinion, very close to being an expanded negative, if it is one

November 25, 1976
Adjournment Motion
that seems to be contained in the proposed motion as the principal reason why the hon. member for Annapolis Valley is opposed to second reading of the bill. They may be valid and interesting reasons, but reasons they are, and in my opinion they do not formulate a statement of a principle which is contrary to the principle of the bill. That is a requirement for a reasoned amendment.
The principle of this bill is very narrow indeed. It is a very specific bill, having to do with restraint of expenditures on certain governmental programs. It seems to me that the very existence of the bill itself indicates that in order to reduce in amplitude the spending programs of the government this bill must be passed by parliament. Therefore the very existence of the bill itself respects the sovereignty of parliament in that regard, and to indicate that a lack of respect is, somehow, a statement of principle contrary to the principles of the bill seems to me irrelevant, considering the restricted nature of the bill itself.
In turn, I might say that the motion could be more properly characterized as an expanded negative reason for opposing the bill at second reading, because it is not declaratory, in my opinion, of a principle contrary to the principle of the bill. Therefore, for these restricted reasons, I cannot accept from a procedural point of view the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley and I rule it out of order.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONVERT IAC INTO CHARTERED BANK
speechtext:
that Bill C-1001, to incorporate Continental Bank of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-1001, an act to incorporate Continental Bank of Canada, would convert IAC Limited into a chartered bank. This bill corresponds to Bill S-30 which was introduced before the Senate on October 28, 1975, passed the Senate and received first and second reading and committee approval in the House of Commons, but did not receive third reading in the House before parliament prorogued. The present bill incorporates the changes to Bill S-30 that were adopted in committee, in the Senate and the House of Commons.
I do not think it is necessary to explain at length the reasons for this bill, but I think it is necessary to outline some salient facts about IAC Limited. Since its founding in 1925, IAC has experienced an enviable growth record so that today it is Canada's eleventh largest financial institution, excluding insurance companies. It has more than 3,000 employees across Canada and over 12,000 shareholders, of whom more than 96 per cent are Canadians. The decision to seek legislation converting it into a chartered bank was made only after detailed study of how IAC could best continue to serve its customers, employees and shareholders in the rapidly changing Canadian financial system. The study concluded that IAC is at a competitive disadvantage by comparison with other financial institutions and that this disadvantage will become of increasing significance as these institutions expand their lending activities in the types of loans made by IAC. In consequence, unless IAC becomes a bank it may be unable to maintain its record of growth or to make optimum use of its equity capital.
IAC concluded that by becoming a bank it will alleviate this competitive disadvantage, put its equity capital to more effective use for its customers, employees and its shareholders, and contribute to competition in the Canadian banking system. These conclusions have been reviewed in light of the recommendations in the white paper on Canadian banking legislation and would not be affected by implementation of those recommendations. Indeed, the reasoning in the white paper corresponds in many ways to the reasoning which led to IAC's conclusion that it should become a bank; further, the conversion of IAC into a bank would directly contribute to the attainment of the policy objectives in the white paper.
It is noteworthy that about 65 per cent of IAC's present business is similar to business done by chartered banks. Over 90 per cent of the business of IAC would be of a type eligible for chartered banks if the white paper's recommendation is implemented that banks be permitted to engage directly in financial leasing services.
November 25, 1976

The conclusion that IAC should become a bank is valid whether or not the white paper proposals are implemented. Indeed, adoption of Bill C-1001 at this time not only would enable IAC to put to more effective use its Canadian-owned equity capital, but also would contribute to the white paper objective of an increase in the number of Canadian banks. On an equity basis, IAC would be the sixth largest Canadian bank. Already, IAC is in competition with the banks in many aspects of its business. With its size, its network of branches in 270 locations across Canada, its established clientele and experienced staff, the additional flexibility made available to it as a bank will enable IAC to compete more effectively with the existing banks. IAC believes that the new Continental Bank will quickly become an important bank serving the clientele established by IAC, expanding that clientele and competing effectively with other banks. Few, if any, of the potential additional entrants into Canadian banking would have a comparable scale of operations or competitive impact.
It is particularly noteworthy that none of the banks chartered within the last five years has available to it resources on the scale available to IAC Limited. In other words, we are seriously interested in providing some competitive clout in the Canadian banking system, and banks we have chartered to date do not have even a fraction of the clout in the Canadian banking system which the chartering of IAC would create.
IAC's equity capital of over $200 million is substantially underutilized in comparison with many other financial institutions. As a major Canadian-owned financial company with a long history of service to the nation's economy, IAC recognizes its responsibility to its shareholders to employ their capital as effectively as possible. IAC has carefully considered the necessity of change in order to enable it to continue its record of success and to serve its customers. Studies conducted with independent advisers indicated that conversion to a chartered bank would enable IAC to improve its ability to serve its established market of individuals and small and medium-size businesses, a service that will be of particular importance during the coming decade when the demands of major resource and industry ventures will place severe strains on Canadian capital markets; attract additional funds from institutional investors and individuals in order to put its Canadian-owned equity capital of more than $200 million to more effective use; broaden the range of financial services that it can provide to its customers through the addition of banking services that IAC is not currently able to provide but which constitute a natural adjunct to its existing activities; contribute to the Canadian economy in the ways described, and be of sufficient size to compete effectively with existing major chartered banks; and put its trained and efficient staff to more effective use.
I shall not comment in detail on the contents of the bill. Hon. members who participated in deliberations of the finance committee during previous sessions of the House are well aware of the details. I commend the bill to the House. I point out that as a result of changes made by the finance committee with respect to the board of directors, IAC has moved to
Continental Bank of Canada
replace all but two of the directors who would be in conflict with the provisions of the existing Bank Act, and those two directors have indicated their willingness to resign the day the bill becomes law. Therefore, the questions raised in committee have been met by IAC and all that remains is to send this bill to the appropriate committee where it can be discussed.
In looking at the question of the white paper on proposed banking legislation and this particular bill, I am told there is nothing in this bill which conflicts with the existing Bank Act, that which is contained in the Bank Act or any of the white paper proposals. Therefore, hon. members ought not to have any problem in terms of dealing with this bill as quickly as possible.
