speechtext:
I withdraw. If the hon. member for Crowfoot says that he did not take a side either way, this is the first time in his life he has done so. He is an outspoken person who does not hesitate to take a stand on any issue. However, I take him at his word and I have no quarrel with that. If it was just a question he was asking, that is fine.
The interest we are expressing in this matter has to go beyond 12,000 shareholders. It has to ask the question of how it affects Canadians generally. It raises some very important issues above the question of the shareholders. It is easy to understand why the shareholders want to convert themselves into a bank. As one of the officers of the bank replied in the finance committee a few weeks ago, "We want to play in the major leagues". I do not hold it against anyone playing in the major leagues, if that is what they want to do. There is no doubt that moving into the major leagues would be immensely profitable for IAC and its shareholders. That is enough reason for them to approve the bid to convert into a bank. But shareholders' profit is not a reason that should be so compelling to parliament. In order for parliament to pass this bill, it should satisfy itself that the bill is in the public interest. Up until this point that has not been demonstrated to me or to my colleagues.
I admire the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I have known him for a long time. I appreciate his sincerity in putting forward his arguments. However, I wish he would have a somewhat better cause than the one he is advocating today.
Let me quote from the Financial Post of April 3, 1976, to reinforce the argument I am trying to make, that the issue of the national interest is not at all clear. If it is not clear to the Financial Post, how can it be clear to anyone? While someone might want to quarrel with my perspective, vision or idea of clarity, surely the vision of clarity of the Financial Post is of a somewhat different order. I quote:
Clearly, the IAC-Continental stall-
That refers to the national interest debate which the NDP is carrying on.
-raises some serious questions for the financial system as a whole-questions that will certainly get important billing during the forthcoming Bank Act debate.
At issue: is it in the public interest for a large, efficient financial organization to convert to a chartered bank? If so, what special arrangements should be permitted to allow for an orderly transition, and what time limit should be set?
If our arguments for waiting until the Bank Act was concluded were valid before, they are even more valid at this point. I imagine within weeks the government will be referring the Bank Act or, more likely, the white paper on banking to the finance committee for examination. If the IAC conversion bill is passed, what is the point of having a debate on the Bank Act? All that IAC is asking for to convert itself into a bank is all contained in the stuff and substance of the debate on the Bank Act. If we pass this bill, we may as well forget about passing the Bank Act.
It is arrogant for a corporation like IAC to come before parliament to ask for special privileges in advance of legislation. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River argued that they are very much in line with the white paper and very much in line with what the government will probably do with amendments to the Bank Act. Therefore, he said, why not let them have it now, rather than wait until the Bank Act is concluded? There are a number of things to be said about that.
What would the hon. member say if in the process of debating a bill to increase the old age pension or amend the Canada Pension Plan a pensioner petitioned this House saying that he had a terrible need and could not wait for the debate to be concluded in parliament as that might take a whole year? He may point out that he has to pay his rent for this month, and as members know, if the bill is passed he would like his cheque right now. I would be far more sympathetic in that case than in this case. This is true of every piece of legislation.
Suppose we were in the process of debating an amendment to the Criminal Code. During the course of that debate, would we instruct the judges, saying that that portion of the Criminal Code is being amended and, therefore, "Do not register any convictions under that section"? That would be an affront to parliament. We would call it arrogant. That is particularly true in this case as it was made quite clear the last time that as far as we were concerned the bill was not going to pass, and we gave our reasons for it.
It bothers me to some extent. I am not the type of person who normally likes to dig in or embarrass anyone or even to say, "Look, I am doing it to inconvenience business." If business comes to me or to other people in my party, we are quite willing to listen and be accommodating to the extent it is possible. If the interests of business and the interests of the country can be demonstrated, we are not going to put up a great fuss. The point is that such a relationship is not clear in this case. There is something about this whole thing that puts me on edge.
What bothers me is that the people in IAC, highly intelligent people, obviously able to run a very large corporation and make a success of it, simply do not understand a darned thing about parliament. They think that if they want something, they can come here and get it without any great debate

November 25, 1976

arising, or they think along these lines: It is going to be debated some time, but what is all this nonsense about holding us up while they get on with their debate? Again, this has not been said to me directly but it has got back to me indirectly. They ask, "Why are you persecuting us?"-as though we were doing something out of vindictiveness. They cannot understand that what they are asking parliament to do is forget about debating the Bank Act and accept the fait accompli.
They have argued in committee that this would in no way set a precedent. Can you imagine letting this bill go through, allowing IAC to convert itself into a bank, holding certain assets and releasing certain other assets, and then, when somebody else comes along asking for the same treatment as IAC, the committee saying, "Oh, no, IAC was all right, but we cannot give the same treatment to you"?
Let me put a hypothesis before you. Suppose the government was satisfied that matters affecting banking corporations ought to be removed from private members' business and that new banks ought to be incorporated in future by letters patent. Would the government introduce this kind of legislation into the House and make it a government bill? Would it dare grant letters patent, knowing it would be called upon to answer questions in the House and explain why enormous concessions had been made to IAC such as had never been made to anyone else, particularly on the eve of amendments to the Bank Act? It is inconceivable to me that a government in its right mind would do such a thing. Yet that is what they are asking private members to do. They are asking us to do some of their dirty work, and we are not going to do it for them.
What is involved in this bill is the very thing we are about to debate in the Bank Act. Should banks be allowed into the leasing field? This is a big question, and not everyone agrees it is a good idea. What are the taxation effects of being able to convert leased assets into other assets? What hidden tax shelters will arise as a consequence? What is the effect of possible conflict of interest, with so many interlocking directorships? What will be the effect of competition? Do we really need competition in the banking system?
The banks and others involved are making a great fuss about the benefits of competition. The chartered banks are saying it is a good idea to have competition. The new entrant says it is a good idea. Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have ever seen established businesses come out to welcome new competition in their field. I have to ask myself, what are the reasons? The banks we have incorporated so far have proven to be non-competitive as far as the established chartered banks are concerned. Though there is no direct relationship, the case for competition has not been made because there has not been any effective competition. In the period in which some of these new banks were being incorporated, the chartered banks have registered the largest profits in their history.
It appears to me that one of the reasons the large, chartered banks welcome competition, or so-called competition, is so that they can say, "We are not a monopoly; we are not dominating the field; there is lots of competition." But the competition has proved to be ineffective. Let me quote a statement by Profes-
Continental Bank of Canada
sor Friedland of York University-this is from the Globe and Mail of November 3. The headline is, "Friedland contends proposed act changes could increase possibility of bank failures". The article reads in part:
The Bank Act changes proposed in the federal government's white paper may have a much more far-reaching impact than is anticipated by either government or deposit-taking institutions, according to Seymour Friedland, professor of finance and economics at York University.
Mr. Friedland suggested that since banks are such an essential part of the Canadian economy it is not clear the same standards of competition should be applied to them as to other industries.
Until now, our banking institutions have been very stable. They have been carefully inspected. If they do not serve the public as well as they might, it is not because of the structure of the banking system but, rather, because of the failure of the government. If interest rates are high, it is not because of the absence of competition but because that is the way the government wants them to be. If there is tight money, it is not because of decisions by the chartered banks but because the government wants it that way. Admitting additional banks into the system will not change that situation. The banking system does not respond in the same competitive way as do other businesses. It responds to the direction and guidance of the Bank of Canada and of the federal government, and the situation would not be changed by admitting the Continental Bank or any other bank.
It would be wrong, in my view, and a disservice to parliament as well as to the debate on the important matters to be dealt with in the amendments to the Bank Act, for us to permit this bill to be passed. This bill should be withdrawn, thus saving the House the time of talking it out and saving the finance committee the trouble of going over the subject again. I realize it might be inconvenient for IAC to wait until the Bank Act has been amended, but the inconvenience to them will be no greater than the inconvenience suffered by other Canadians who are obliged to stand in the wings and wait until parliament reaches a decision upon one matter or another. At present, IAC is saying, "We cannot wait for parliament. We have 12,000 shareholders who are more important than debates in parliament or decisions parliament is taking." Such an attitude should find no reflection here.

Mr. Speaker, circumstances have us discuss banking problems once again. Inevitably our banking system implies the word "credit". In a system the like of which we now live in, loans are made specially in the form of credit entries to the borrower in the bank's books. A loan creates new credit that did not exist before the loan. I feel it is quite normal, under the circumstances, to underline to some extent the workings of the banking mechanism which contributed and still does to the creation of a feeling of anxiety among the peoples of various lands. Here, in Canada, we are at grips with a system like that one, and before supporting a bill that recommends the setting

November 25, 1976
Continental Bank of Canada
up of a new bank, it is wise to pause and glance at what that system produces.
As I was saying, a loan creates new credit that did not exist previously. That credit has all the virtues of solid money; it circulates through the cheques the borrower signs to make payments; it is withdrawn from circulation by the sale of goods, through the taxes levied by public bodies or in reimbursements to the bank to wipe out the loan. If the rhythm and volume of loans exceed that of the reimbursements, credit expands, and therefore more money circulates. If, on the contrary, the rhythm and volume of reimbursements exceed that of loans, less money circulates. That decrease can be the result of harsher conditions imposed upon the borrowers through higher interest rates or simply, by refusing to lend; that is what is known as compressing or restricting credit, which is the main form of money in the modern world.
Financial credit depends mainly on the action taken by banks, central or commercial, it does not matter much which type of bank we intend to set up. If true credit is a social credit, therefore financial credit is a bank credit. Let us not forget that no Financial credit is possible without true credit. The money used to pay producers and production would be of no use if there were no producers or production. Real credit, the country's capacity to produce, is the real basis and the only value warranty of financial credit. People seem to have a hard time understanding this, yet it is so perfectly clear.
And since true credit is a common good, a social good, financial credit, in order to mobilize it and redistribute its profits, should be in the hands of society. To me, it is easy to understand. Control of financial credit by profit-making institutions is an usurpation and the usurper acts as dictator when he refuses the financial credit necessary to establish true credit. The capacity to produce is then hampered by the inability to pay. The capacity to produce depends on the country and on its population; the inability to pay depends on the inadequacy of financial credit.
Thus, the production of goods manufactured to meet human needs is subject to the decisions of the banking system, and is either facilitated, hindered or completely prohibited, according to its actions. This is a dictatorial system, our entire economic life depends on its decisions. Those who control money and credit hold our lives in their hands. You probably already know who said it, and he knew what he was saying then. I think it would be in order now to recall what a former Prime Minister of Canada used to say, and you know him it was the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King who said: Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation.
Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and democracy is idle and futile. I will carry on with another quotation taken from a former President of the United States, Lincoln's monetary policy summarized and certified by the Library of Congress: The government should create, issue
and circulate all the currency required to satisfy the spending power of the government and the buying power of consumers. The privilege of creating and issuing money is not only the supreme prerogative of government, it is the government's greatest creative opportunity to create wealth.
In modern time money is nothing more than an item of accountancy. But this accounting is wrong and does not correspond to reality. We have a fraudulent Financial system which does not Fit with our real needs and possibilities. When a banker makes a loan he creates money based on the work of the producer who is the one who really creates wealth. The banker creates figures, puts into debt the wealth producer, although he is the one who supplies our goods. He gets him into debt for a greater value than the produced wealth, since the producer must add to his debt the interests which he owes on it. What nonsense! This is why the more a country is developed, the more it is collectively in debt to financiers who do nothing. We have reached that point in Canada.
Since I have been elected here in 1962, I no longer hear members in the House dealing with Financial matters and steps they would take to pay our national debt. We do not hear about that. All their efforts are centered on ways to pay the interests-

We live in a system in which we must pay financially during 20 years, three times the value of what we received once physically. Why that reluctance to change a system that gives us such bad results? Money does not come out of the sky. It is manufactured, controlled and rarefied by men. We must be able to make a well oriented decision that will allow us to find a place for everything and put everything in its place but money is a way to allow the goods to meet the needs, provided those who make it or handle it take into consideration the value of the human person and the right of everyone to live. We are seeing all sorts of inflationary and deflationary situations; governments are fighting what they helped create, inflation, when they manage or think they can manage to arrest or curb it, to use a well known expression.

I am quite aware of the powers held by banks and I am not very favourable to the creation of other institutions like this. As I already told the House, I think, I have never forgiven the system that kept us during 10 years in the famous depression of the thirties when people of my age were quite prepared to look after their own future by trying to organize their life according to their aspirations, but the answer that union representatives or others received from the government of that time was: "We lack money." Always the lack of money. Why do we not try to find a way to resolve that problem? As I said earlier, it is a fact that no one can deny, money is not a godsend; it is made, handled by men. Why is humanity not able to put some order in this chaotic system?
According to clause 75 of the legislation, we see that banks enjoy several privileges. Paragraph D mentions: "acquire, deal in, discount and lend money and make advances upon the security of bills of exchange..Most members know or should know that banks are entitled to make loans 10 to 12 times higher than the amount they have on hand and the currency they have in deposit at the Bank of Canada. bers' bills, there is always a team on the government's side ready to prevent the adoption of those bills.
When it comes to bills related to the creation of new banks, I can see that government members seem rather in favour of their adoption.
Consequently, I think that most people seem ready to bow as usual to the wizards of finance. The government of a country, the body which has the power to legislate, should be willing to create a sound domestic economy. This is what should be. We could give many examples of the implications of the present loan system. Public buildings, bridges, roads have been paid three times. You cannot contradict me, I have facts, I have evidence with me. Bridges, roads have been paid three times because of the present loan system of the banks. Costly wars have been won, costly wars as far as lives and equipment was concerned. We had to pay for them years after they had ended. This is simply illogical. The very understanding mayor of a town in our province, a man at grips with a constant debt problem, summarized not so long ago what had happened when bonds for a total of $573,500 were issued. First the town had to pay $17,211.60 in brokerage fees and $2,051.15 for the printing of the bonds, to which were added the legal fees. Furthermore, the discount cost $17,000. When the first instalment of that loan will be redeemed, an amount of $486,000, they will have to pay, on top of that sum, a total interest of $494,157.50. So, over a period of 40 years, this form of financing which gives the town less than $475,000 in real terms will have cost $980,157.50. And we still use such systems.
Interests and charges more than double the cost of the loan. The people are now realizing that their elected representatives in Parliament or provincial legislatures must be changed, if they cannot do anything with a system that has been eating us continuously.
The Bank of Canada should take the initiative on such a service, to cut in half the cost of municipal loans. The Social Credit Party has been urging this throughout Canada for a long time. He will have to be patient and wait until I finish because it will take me a few more minutes. I am pleased to be allowed to continue my speech. A large part of the public debt is to be paid to chartered banks. Everybody knows that a $1,000 Canada savings bond constitutes a reserve for the private banking system through which they can loan up to 16 times the amount of that $1,000 savings bond. Therefore, the bank is entitled to grant $16,000 in loans thanks to this $1,000 bond. This is clear enough, I think. Nobody will challenge that, it is the law that allows it.
The major portion of the debt is directly payable to chartered banks. I recall that several years ago I asked a minister of finance to whom were Canadians indebted. In reply, he sent me a letter saying that it was difficult to answer exactly such a question and he poured out a lot of statistics. When I showed this letter to people, they could not believe what I had been telling them and concluded that even the Minister of Finance of Canada was unable to prove and explain to whom Canadians are indebted. They said that is why we are so concerned about such debts, because even the Minister of Finance does not know to whom we owe money.
The major portion of the debt is directly payable to chartered banks. Here is how it works: The government issues a bond of $1 billion or $1 million. The Bank of Canada buys it outright and credits the government's account. This immediately creates a reserve for the private banking industry which is entitled to multiply by 16, that is to grant $16 million credit on $1 million collateral. Then the government borrows five or six additional million dollars, loaned by a private bank and generated by the private banking industry. Later the Bank of Canada will be responsible for only $1 million as a guarantee for the new credits by chartered banks.
While the man in the street gets his money through his work, banks generate their money through a procedure which does not cost them anything except ink, a writing pen and a clerk. The Bank of Canada states that figures have to be set, and the government does set them. The only thing which is to be paid for is the salary of the clerk. They create money by means which cost them virtually nothing. The issue at stake is to determine who is running the country. Parliament was not elected to serve banks. We were all elected to serve our voters, the Canadian people and our country. We are here to serve Canada.
We must drag Canada out of the claws of financiers who are devouring it. That is what we must do. So let us take the necessary means. This is not in any way a matter of partisanship. What we are proposing is an economic system which is sound, based on something true and which would prevent Canadians from fighting among themselves and arguing whether we must get ready or not, whether we must think this or that, whether we should start endless strikes, whether our governments will be able to settle them with pieces of legislation which complicate matters instead of improving them, and which will teach Canadians to work together for the progress of their country.
As Social Crediters, we make suggestions. If the government and a number of hon. members do not seem to agree with them, let us hope they will find reasonably good means to put some order in the current chaos. Otherwise the situation would not make sense and could not continue.
To give you an example, in conclusion, on March 25, 1976 a citizen from the Sherbrooke area wrote a letter to Le Soleil, and I quote:

Through the action of interest, a huge financial web surrounds and binds us more and more, leaving us only with our lives ... or barely.
Snowballing, the interest accumulates and centralizes the money in the hands of a small group of financiers. The interest. . . this parasite which has never lifted a shovelful of dirt to build a country, steals, takes without producing and is added to the price of goods, which is the cause of ever increasing prices and inflation today.

We are talking about Bill C-19. We are talking about restraint. Would the hon. member like to get up on a point of order?
Right there, in this House on the record on page 1274 the Prime Minister showed his utter disregard for sound administration. He revealed his swimming pool syndrome which is very evident here and so is the Sky Shops syndrome still prominent in this Trudeau liberalism of mismanagement and "blow the works", "spend money". That is all their policy amounts to. The Prime Minister's philosophy is now "To hell with the auditors and chartered accountants"-and that is tantamount to what he said at page 1274 of Hansard. He added that "our institution does not necessarily have to be run the way accountants say it should."
I challenge the Prime Minister on this, Mr. Speaker. Take away audits and auditors, which is the apparent present Liberal policy, and there is nothing left on which you can depend. There would be almost instant bankruptcy of the country. Liberal credibility is at an all time low but it would be lower if audits were taken away.
The government did not like Mr. Henderson because of his strict findings and stringent opinions, so it moved him out and appointed Mr. Macdonell. He is doing the traditionally good job of all auditors general and is serving parliament and the Canadian people well. I say thank God there is an Auditor General doing his duty. He declares that fiscal control by this government has almost vanished.
I say to the Prime Minister that this institution must be run along the lines of strict, direct, sound and solvent accountancy, not the way he infers at page 1274 of Hansard. The ethics and laws which govern the profession of accountancy are quite a bit above those of politicians and most other walks of life. I would remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that a politician can lie, and a merchant or farmer or any other non-professional- even a preacher-can lie if they should be foolish and deceptive enough to do so, but an accountant, chartered or otherwise, in carrying out his duties cannot lie. That is why Mr. Henderson never lied to this House or the Canadian people, and neither did Mr. Macdonell. They cannot misrepresent. Should an accountant misrepresent anything, his credibility and his business are finished. He must report the fiscal and financial truth and that is what has been revealed this week to the Canadian people.
I say again to the Prime Minister that he should take note of this. Last Tuesday he referred to matters of political science and the parliamentary system when he said that we do not have to heed accountants. Neither political science nor the parliamentary system can endure without strict accounting by honest, unbiased accountants.
I should like to refer to some of the comment of the day on this matter, Mr. Speaker. The Montreal Gazette is certainly not a Conservative newspaper; I believe it is basically Liberal in thought and doctrine. This morning's edition had this to say:
The Trudeau government has become mere grease for the mandarin machine that runs the Canadian public administration. Parroting old speeches of top civil servants, Prime Minister Trudeau told the House of Commons the reverse of the

truth when he said appointment of a financial comptroller would detract from parliamentary control of public spending. The truth is, rather, as Auditor General J. J. Macdonnell stated it: a comptroller-general would be responsible through a minister to parliament, enabling parliament to keep tighter financial control.
Prime Minister Trudeau is feeding the Commons a diet of solid red herring when he again parrots the mandarins and says government cannot be run like private business. The mandarinate, whose incompetence in financial management has been uncovered by Mr. Macdonnell, has reacted as though to a takeover bid by private industry. Baloney. What Mr. Macdonnell demanded was the following:
"A financial plan that serves as a cornerstone for managing and controlling financial resources.
"A central system of budgetary control, based on effectively functioning control systems in each department and agency.
"Complete and appropriate financial reports.
That is something we never get any more in question period, and we cannot even get them by resorting to the order paper. The editorial continues:
"Effective financial control based on a system of continuous and automatic checks on expenditure decisions."
What better could parliament want as a means or gaining accountability from the government? It is not to big business that government and parliament are losing control over spending, it is to big bureaucracy.
The final sentence of the editorial refers to the actions of the government in its stopgap efforts to put on a show of finally trying to bring our financial condition under control. It reads:
It is enough to make a taxpayer puke.
That is the opinion of most Canadian people. When the Prime Minister put on a new suit and went on television to speak about what happened last week in Quebec, he was only putting up a smokescreen to divert attention from the country's disastrous financial condition, a condition resulting from Liberal mismanagement and poor policies of the past decade. We do not need to worry about Quebec. When they next vote the people of Quebec will be just as prudent with regard to the future of Canada and their future in Canada as they were last week when they repudiated Liberalism. I congratulate the people of Quebec on the latter action.
In the early days of the present government members on both sides of the House used to greet announcements of fiscal restraint with good natured banter. Somehow such announcements made us laugh, but only before the Prime Minister pulled out all the stops and went on an uncontrolled spending spree which is now completely out of hand. The Auditor General in his report said earlier this week that the government has lost effective control over spending in our country. I am afraid it is long past the time when we could laugh at the government's ineptitude and fiscal irresponsibility.
If there were one iota of evidence to be garnered from Bill C-19 showing it will lead to fiscal restraint such as hon. members opposite were claiming a few minutes ago, I cannot imagine any member of the House voting against it. We have reached the point at which we must save every dollar; even so, this country will be dismally in the red. We in this House, and Canadians everywhere, are getting ever more alarmed at the
November 25, 1976

recklessness of the present government, particularly of some of its ministers. If ever a Prime Minister of Canada regarded the public purse as his own private reserve, it is the present one. He has imbued his ministers with the spirit of reckless abandon in the spending of public tax moneys. When the Prime Minister himself shrugs his shoulders and greets any comments on his fiscal recklessness with a glib remark and leaves the impression that "It's only money", we can expect his hand-picked, buddies, and party hacks to respond in the same way when they get their own hands on the public purse.
The Prime Minister must have suffered a great shock on the evening of November 15 when he discovered that the billions of dollars he had lavished on Quebec over the years had not bought the respect and support of the people of that province. His way is not the way of assuring the respect and support of right thinking people. It must have been a great let down when he discovered that the spending of billions of dollars on his ill-conceived bilingualism program in English Canada has not impressed or fooled anyone, either in English Canada or in Quebec.
One can only hope that the Prime Minister now will take time to review programs such as bilingualism; in these areas we can save billions of dollars without cutting back on social programs with which we are at least doing some good. I might add that we can do this without cutting back bilingual service where it is needed in this country. When fiscal restraint means that we have to cut into programs which are assisting Canadians in need of help, we are being penny wise and pound foolish. Of course you may not hear people talking about being "pound foolish" in future if the pound continues to lose value. That is not fiscal restraint. It is fiscal confusion, in many cases fiscal foolishness.
The shaving of funds from social programs should not be attempted in an omnibus bill such as the one we are considering, in any event, Mr. Speaker. We are considering a bill which is to give official and final sanction to the demise of two agencies, Information Canada and the Company of Young Canadians. I think we can well dispense with them. Those agencies have been dead for several months and, as some in this debate have already said, good riddance to both. But it was not really necessary or even proper to try to lend dignity to Bill C-19 by throwing in, as it were, those two dead agencies. A short bill to bring about the official end of those agencies could have been introduced at any time. I doubt if anyone would want to waste time debating such an issue except, possibly, a couple of members of the NDP.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) called on the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) last week to remove from Bill C-19 those portions dealing with the Railway Act so that they could be debated separately. I thought it was a good idea. However, I am sure that the hon. member knew that this government is not going to do anything so rational or reasonable as to allow us to debate bills containing only related and complementary issues. Omnibus bills are more to the liking of this government and, as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) noted earlier, this government is
Restraint of Government Expenditures "hung up" on bills which are open-ended, in which the blanks are filled in after the bills secure passage through the House.
We have seen all too often how the government uses omnibus bills. We are debating an omnibus bill at present. Frankly I do not think the government should try to amend the Railway Act with an omnibus bill. The Railway Act should not be amended as the government intends to do it. Passage of the amendment will mean, for one thing, more expensive feed grains in eastern Canada and Quebec, and more expensive western feed grain east of the Lakehead.
When the government introduces an omnibus bill, it sweetens the bill by throwing in a couple of things which appeal to the majority of members; then the government sits back and waits for us to object to the onerous parts of the bill. When we complain that it is a bad bill the Prime Minister says, "Oh, I thought you wanted to get rid of Information Canada; I thought you wanted to get rid of the Company of Young Canadians." The answer is that we do want to get rid of both those agencies. Mercifully, we are already rid of them. I object to having them used at this date as red herrings to allow the government to get out of still more cost-sharing programs involving provincial governments. The government seeks to do this in the way it weaseled out of shared-cost medicare and hospital programs a few months ago with Bill C-68.
I also object to the ministers' self-righteous claim about how much money will be saved with the passage of Bill C-19. Sir, we are all well aware why the Prime Minister established Information Canada. It enabled the Prime Minister to pay off a number of party faithful in one fell swoop. We know that those people have since been shifted into equally well paid positions, many of them sinecures, no doubt. Certainly there is no reason for our supposing that we are saving nearly as much as the minister claims. Information Canada was the absolute epitome of senseless duplication of effort and an appalling waste of tax moneys. I for one hope that we have seen not only the last of Information Canada, but the last of any such agencies of government.
I want just as much to be rid once and for all of outfits like the Company of Young Canadians; but there are still some unanswered questions about the CYC, as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka pointed out in his remarks earlier. I want to know how the Company of Young Canadians, or at least the officers of that group, were able to get so close to the public purse. I want to know how they were able to pay themselves $185,000 out of the public treasury, under the nose of the minister responsible for the CYC, when it was known that the CYC Act did not authorize any such payments. It was also known that this occurred after the date the Company of Young Canadians was supposed to be disbanded.

speechtext: Just a bunch of young Grits.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Yes, it is a very easy way to get money out of the Trudeau government. If the responsible minister was aware that these payments were being made and in fact

November 25, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
authorized such payments, he should be brought before a committee of this House. Of course it is not Liberal policy to do that. They prefer to name another royal commission and spend more millions of dollars.
If the minister did not take steps to prevent the payments being made, he in fact authorized the payments with his failure to act. If that is the case, the minister should be forced to resign. Unfortunately, it would not be punishment for a misdeed because we know only too well the minister would be brought back into the cabinet within a few days or weeks. He would then hold a press conference and chide his colleagues in the House of Commons who were so naive as to believe he could be kept out of the cabinet.
I would like to renew my call for a complete and thorough investigation of the activities of the Canadian International Development Agency. I asked for this months ago. If the government is interested in fiscal restraint, here is one area where it can get some results.
I do not see how it can object to parliament being informed as to just what Mr. Gerin-Lajoie is doing with the billion dollars of Canadian tax money, he is being allowed to dispense each year in countries of the "Third World". Gerin-Lajoie has too much of a free hand, and in my view too much of a good thing, being allowed to spend that kind of money without a dollar-by-dollar accounting to parliament.
According to a reliable and completely unimpeachable source, the Auditor General, this government has too many little agencies and corporations acting as though they can have access to the public treasury without having to account for their actions.
Not long ago the salaries of members of parliament were cut back. We are still repaying that portion that it is claimed we should not have received. I and other members are willing to do this. We are not kicking about it. We want the financial books of Canada to be in the black and to be properly handled and balanced.
As I say, we are all accountable, and the Prime Minister cannot be allowed to continue this charade of his, appointing an army of cronies to sensitive posts in the government, telling them in effect that they can spend from the public treasury and just tell any inquisitive members of parliament to mind their own business if they ask too many prying questions. Well, Mr. Speaker, prying into the multitude of questionable uses of public funds happens to be my business, and since we are talking today about fiscal restraint I should put another little thought into the record. I have a very suspicious mind when it comes to political patronage, nepotism, and cronyism, especially of the type practised so widely by the present Prime Minister and the Liberal party.
I do not feel comfortable knowing that there are so many people who have a key to the public treasury without a corresponding level of accountability. Revelations by the Auditor General certainly brought that forward this past week. I am sure all members of parliament feel uncomfortable about so many people having a key to the public treasury without a

corresponding measure of accountability. If I am asked a direct question as to whether I question the integrity of some of those people appointed by the present government, the answer is an unqualified yes.
I question the integrity, and the judgment of many of those who are presently in a position where they can authorize expenditures of tax moneys. A look at some of the items left out of annual fiscal reports and accounts, as documented by the Auditor General, and some of the fictitious listings in some other reports and accounts, would lead any reasonable person to believe that there is something seriously wrong in the public service of our country.
With regard to the CANDU deals, about $10 million is missing. No one knows where it went or for what purpose. So far there is no indication that that amount was ever audited.
Before I run out of time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address myself to the clause in Bill C-19 that will allow the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) to exercise the kind of latitude in the field of adult training that the ministers of this government insist on having. The ministers across the floor do not want to tackle a cabinet post unless they are allowed to make up their own ground rules as they bungle along from day to day. That statement is true. This government has bungled along for eight years.
For the past eight years we have had an ad hoc government, with no long range plans, no set rules of conduct, and no conception of what would be best for the majority of the people in our country. In fact where this government is concerned, its members themselves are the country, and they themselves are the only people whose interests matter. As an old French king once said, "l'etat, c'est moi".
With regard to the matter of adult training, I believe that it is time now to rethink the whole matter, to accept the fact that it should be considered a brand new ball game, and write a new set of rules. This process should take into account that there are two major or significant classifications of unemployed, the skilled and the unskilled.
I had a case last week. I am sure other members have had similar experiences. A young lady called me. She stated that the local Manpower office had enrolled her in a retraining course, hairdressing. She was very anxious to have that training. After having enrolled at the school, she returned to the Manpower office to get their O.K. They then told her they were very sorry, and that even though she had enrolled and was ready to begin the course, this could not be done because they did not have any money. That is great service to the Canadian people.
We should take into account that there are basically two classifications of employer in the private sector, the large industries and small businesses. Many of the speeches that I have made in this House and in my riding have touched on the subject of small businesses, and the fact that at least 50 per cent of wage earners in Canada are employed by small businesses.
November 25, 1976

I am glad to see that a minister has been appointed to look after small business. If he is given the encouragement and support he deserves, he will very likely improve the lot of small business in Canada. I myself was in a small business for 25 years before I was elected to parliament. My hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka has stated that if all small businesses in Canada were to close down suddenly the country would come to a standstill. That is true. And that is why the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand) has a tremendous responsibility. I think he deserves the support which the nature of his portfolio warrants. If there were no small business, not only would the public be deprived of a tremendous variety of services now available to them, and largely taken for granted, but there would be a dramatic increase in unemployment levels.
At the present time there are approximately three quarters of a million people without jobs in Canada. That is what Statistics Canada says. I believe, in my own mind, that there are at least one million people unemployed in Canada today, because in addition to the 750,000 who are registered there is a faceless mass of people-we do not know their numbers- who are no longer eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. No record is kept of them, and I do not think the government is interested in knowing how many there are because the figure would be a further embarrassment to it. The present level is scandalous, not only because so many people are out of work but because the government seems incapable of devising any orderly action to deal with the situation.
I sometimes wonder whether our millionaire Prime Minister fancies himself as a latter day Marie Antoinette, raying with an arrogant shrug of his shoulders that if thousands of Canadians are without bread, let them eat cake. It is a different matter, though, if it happens to be a crony of the Prime Minister. In that case, anything goes. Let him have the key to the public treasury and tell parliament to stop harassing him with silly requests for accounting and accountability. But to get back to the subject of unemployment and adult retraining, I have some thoughts on the matter and I will use my remaining time in which to express them.
As I mentioned earlier, there are two classes of unemployed, in the main, and two classes of employer. In the case of the small business employer, we can assist him by helping him to get started, helping him to survive, and helping him to expand. Today the government is doing quite the opposite. It harasses small business to the point at which increasing numbers of them are packing it in. Thousands of small businessmen have given up over the past eight or ten years, and you cannot really blame them. It is only within a healthy, growing economy, one in which industry and small business can thrive, that we shall be able to put people to work if they really want to work.
On one hand we must provide industry with a continuing supply of skilled labour, and on the other hand put in place a program capable of providing industry with a pool of young
Restraint of Government Expenditures
people who have demonstrated their ability to absorb and apply the levels of skill needed by industry. The most practical way to train people to work in the trades is to develop a co-ordinated program involving industry and the Department of Manpower. The only people who really know what is required by way of skills and training are the people who actually do the hiring.
We have seen too many examples of the folly of allowing bureaucrats sitting in their offices in Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto to decide how training programs are set up and what trades are to be emphasized. All too often we see programs set up to train people for jobs which do not exist, or to train two or three people for every single job available in a given trade group or specialty.
The answer is a broader program of on-the-job training. We must take care to train people for jobs which actually exist, and for jobs which have a good chance of lasting more than a couple of months. We have had enough of the government's ad hoc make-work programs which provide low paying jobs enabling people to do their own thing for two or three months before rejoining the ranks of the unemployed. Every industrialized country in the western world, with the exception of Canada, has in place a co-ordinated on-the-job training program, an on-going program, which ensures that from day to day and month to month industries have available to them the types of skill they need in order to operate and expand.
Mr. Speaker, this bill requires considerable amendment before it is worthy of passage. I support the amendment put forward by my hon. friend from Lambton-Kent.

Mr. Speaker, my ideas on Bill C-19 have changed, I have to admit, since it was first introduced. There are many segments of our society that have forced these changes and I think that people are probably more aware of the government's hurry to get this bill through. We shall probably have to stop to cover up some of the folly in government management spending.
I shall probably be asked to be a party to giving parliamentary approval to the write-off of almost $6 million in questionable loans and advances from the federal treasury, and I can say now it will be against everything I believe in with respect to good business practice and sound government. I refer to the $2.8 billion advanced to the unemployment insurance account, to the $2.4 billion in loans to certain Crown corporations, and $1.2 billion in loans to developing countries. This represents part of a large percentage of the total national budget which the Auditor General states was misspent. Along with this I would mention too the $800,000 which was spent for a boat which would not float. We could make many snide references with respect to this boat costing $800,000, which would not float. We shall probably talk about that later on. All these sums were inadequately accounted for last year out of a total budget of $42 billion.

November 25, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
The Canadian government is the largest corporation in our country. 1 ask this House what corporation could survive with such questionable financial practices, such sloppy accounting procedures, and such arrogant disregard for principle and integrity?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in keeping with the practice of this House I will keep to the principle of the bill being debated. I will address myself to a number of specific items that fall within the broad category of fiscal restraint, in order to please the hon. gentleman from whom we should like to hear.
Let me refer to areas of activity where gasoline is necessary for the operation and the conduct of business. I am sure that were the hon. gentleman to speak for some of the businessmen in his community he could make the same remarks. This additional tax on gasoline is hurting industry whether it be in western Ontario, central Ontario, eastern Ontario or, for that matter, in northern Ontario. Tourism in Ontario is the second largest segment of our provincial economy. Nationally it is the fourth largest segment accounting for $1 in every $18 of the gross national product. Let me read briefly from a speech delivered by the Hon. C. Bennett, the Ontario Minister of Tourism. He stated:
The economy has slipped over the past few years, and you don't need to tell me that you are feeling the effects, if not actually hurting. Your prosperity, based as it is on leisure time and on the patronage of such people as sales representatives, is perhaps more vulnerable than that of any other service sector. When companies and individuals cut back, you feel it first. You are a part of an extremely important industry-tourism-which in dollar terms comes fourth in Canada after automobiles, oil and gas, and wheat, which contributes almost $8 billion a year to the national economy. That's about one dollar in eighteen of the gross national product. In the province of Ontario, tourism is the second largest industry, and last year it generated $2.6 billion. This year (1976) we expect it to increase slightly, and achieve a level of $2.8 billion, of which $900 million will come from other countries.
In the larger perspective, damage to Ontario's tourist industry affects Canada's balance of payments. Ontario is in relatively good shape, but let us look at the national deficit. Between 1974 and 1975 this deficit, both U.S. and overseas,

grew from $284 million to $706 million. If the trend continues this country may soon be a billion dollars in the red on the tourism account.
Having regard to the United States account, in 1974 Canada had a $132 million surplus with the U.S. This dropped last year to a deficit of over $234 million. In 1976 this deficit could double. In a nutshell, too few Americans are visiting Canada and too many Canadians are visiting the United States. This has to be turned around. The provincial Minister of Tourism has indicated that he plans to recommend at the upcoming federal-provincial conference that the provinces, regional associations, and the private sector assume full responsibility for domestic advertising.
Let me refer to the ten cents excise tax on gasoline to which I referred earlier. Granting the fact that moneys were needed to balance out the price of oil between Canadian provinces, I believe this ten cents per gallon tax imposed upon a vital and already heavily taxed commodity has already hurt many industries in Canada. We are told that the government hopes to raise $350 million through this tax. The government could have raised money less painfully, and without hurting our businesses and industries, simply by using some common sense in managing the country's finances. The Auditor General gives scores of examples. Let me point out some of them.
First there are these questionable payments to unknown foreign agents to promote the sale of CANDU atomic reactors. These payments amounted to tens of millions of dollars. Perhaps it is worth mentioning that our major allies have questioned Canada's practice of selling atomic reactors to countries that do not guarantee that the reactors will not be used for the manufacture of atomic weapons.
Secondly, there is the questionable and inefficient use of public moneys for travel and relocation expenses, some $200 million. These are expenses that have not been properly identified. As the Auditor General reported, the guidelines for spending money for these purposes were "either inconsistently applied, or substantially ignored".
Untold millions of dollars are being wasted or misspent since, in the words of the Auditor General, "financial management and control is not a priority within Crown corporations". The Auditor General stated further that financial management and control in Crown corporations are grossly inadequate.
We are all aware that the House of Commons is known as the senior branch of government in Canada, followed by many lesser bodies at the provincial and various municipal levels. Having had the privilege of being a member of a municipal government I often wonder how long such a government would be allowed to carry on if it proceeded in the same manner as the federal government in respect of financial management. I may say at this time that while the municipal governments in Canada handle far less money, the business practice is much more efficient, and there is a great deal more scrutiny by fewer people. A municipal council cannot spend even $1,000 today without being questioned. Yet this government spends millions of dollars for which it cannot account.
November 25, 1976

Let me refer now to the increased cost of agricultural production. We all know many factors contribute to this increased cost of productivity, including the ten cents excise tax on gasoline. We are all aware of the monumental problems facing those involved in agriculture today. Instead of providing a metric calendar and questionable humour regarding the effects of eating too much beef, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) would do better to concern himself with promoting the consumption of Canadian agricultural products.
The recent revelation today by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurlburt), in a proposed motion under Standing Order 43, that Air Canada's tender for beef calls for Australian or New Zealand beef rather than Canadian is astounding. This is inexcusable.
We have a government which on the one hand squanders billions and on the other hand ignores the Canadian producer in an attempt supposedly to save a few cents per pound on foreign beef. Crown corporations should set the example in promoting Canadian products. This certainly should include the agricultural sector.
Another thing I should like to bring to the attention of the government is something about which I am sure the minister and many other members on the government benches are aware. I refer to the cost to the farmer of producing beef. That cost today is 50 cents a pound. It requires about eight pounds of grain to produce one pound of livestock. This beef sells on the market in Toronto at from 38 cents to 48 cents a pound. In other words the farmer is losing six cents to eight cents a pound by producing and selling beef on the Canadian market today. How long can the agricultural industry stand such a situation? In my opinion the agricultural industry today is living off its depreciation. How long can we have a viable industry in Canada with this situation? Members of the agricultural community have lost animals and I do not think they have been adequately compensated under the health of animals legislation, but no one sees fit on the government side to do anything about this.
I recall that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in reply to a question, stated that Mr. Caron is a worthy individual who has contributed much to this country as a member of royal commissions. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that thousands of other Canadians have contributed as much as Mr. Caron, and probably for far less remuneration. These Canadians have made their contribution for the good of the country and ask very little in return. I cannot help but wonder about this matter and the question raised by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the House yesterday. He asked whether Mr. Lambert had been appointed to the recently announced royal commission because of his desire to control salary levels, he having previously recommended that deputy ministers should be paid up to $60,000 a year. He also wondered whether Mr. Stoner was being appointed because he was the former deputy minister of transport during the Sky Shops affair.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
Under these circumstances, general platitudes assuring the House of the noted competence of these individuals is far from reassuring. I suggest it is now too late for a royal commission to be appointed. What is required and what is owing to the Canadian people is a full judicial inquiry. Such an inquiry could consider the specific instances of waste and mismanagement referred to in the Auditor General's report. Some of the money which has been misspent could be given to the small businessman who still employs 60 per cent of the labour force in Canada.
The small businessman is supposed to have access to guaranteed loans, but when he goes to the bank, especially in the province of Ontario, he finds that this money is not available. The bankers say that when they can loan money for ten per cent, 12 per cent or 13 per cent, why should they loan it to the small businessman when all that is permitted under the government's guidelines is 8 per cent? The government has forgotten about the small businessman in Canada. In the province of Ontario this situation is even more acute than it probably is anywhere else.
There is a question I should like to ask the minister in charge of DREE. In the last few days I have attempted to ask this question in the House of Commons. Will he expand on the criteria that govern whether or not an area is included under the DREE grants?
Now I should like to return to the question I mentioned earlier and said I would come back to in respect of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not find too much fault with the people who are involved in the implementation of the act in the local offices, but there are a few things 1 should like to bring to the attention of the government. Some of these matters where drawn to the attention of the government by myself as long ago as 18 months, but nothing has been done about them. The fact is that claimants for unemployment insurance continue to be penalized under the four-week nil pay clause legislation. This involves a case where someone who is receiving unemployment insurance in good faith voluntarily withdraws, possibly because he is absent from the area or otherwise. He receives no pay for four weeks. He is still disqualified according to his contributions and stamps, and when he returns to apply again for benefits from the commission, because of four weeks nil pay he is disqualified.
I brought that situation to the attention of the government 18 months ago and nothing was done about it. Last June I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration about people being called in from long distances. Some offices were processing over 600 people a week. I call it a harassment program. These people were called in each week, and I think the intention was that eventually they would become tired of coming in and would discontinue claiming unemployment insurance benefits. The hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) also referred to this matter. He said there were untold numbers of unemployed about whom we probably know nothing. The government has been made aware of this situation by opposition members but it has failed, as it has in respect of many other things, to take action.
